# Game 1: Black vs 9d — W+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, White komi 7, simple ko.
Black resigned after move 56, White D2. No numerical final score was produced.
The opponent was the strongest available human-style profile. This was a baseline, not a calibrated training level.

## Full record
- game-001.sgf: standard SGF, all 56 stone moves.
- game-001-log.json: tool responses including every board and final resignation.
- Final captures: Black 2, White 2. Final ko point: D1.

## Main strategic failure
Black occupied the center and connected many stones, but White obtained the left and right sides. Center influence did not become enough area or a productive attack. By the middle game, the rough territorial count was clearly losing even assuming the main Black chain survived.

The opening was:
1 B E5, 2 W C5, 3 B E3, 4 W D7, 5 B F7, 6 W G5,
7 B G6, 8 W H6, 9 B G7, 10 W G3, 11 B C3, 12 W C6.
Black's upper-right contact exchanges let White establish the right side. This is an observation about the resulting position, not proof that a particular opening move was objectively inferior. Earlier C3 or a more territorial response to G5 are candidates for future manual study.

## Concrete tactical error: the upper cut
31 B D8, 32 W C8 put D8 in atari.
33 B E9, 34 W D9 captured D8.
I had considered capturing E8 with F8, but overlooked that removing D8 opened a NEW liberty at D8 for White E8. E9 itself was also in atari after White D9, so 35 B F9 was needed to extend it.

Later, 49 B F8 put E8 in atari. White played 50 J7, allowing 51 B D8 to capture E8. This created a ko at E8 rather than a secure new eye: Black D8 had only E8 as a liberty.
The lesson is to account for liberties exposed by removed stones, and distinguish a ko capture from unconditional life.

## Life-and-death failure
The central chain had almost no internal eye space. At the end:
- G9 was a genuine enclosed eye point.
- D2 was an apparent lower eye whose border stone D1 was isolated and in atari after White E1.
- E8 was an apparent upper eye whose border stone D8 was isolated and in atari.
- Filling either D2 or E8 to connect the vulnerable stone would consume that eye space.

55 B J9 gained the corner point, but 56 W D2 captured D1 and started a ko at D1.
Black was already far behind in area and had no identified adequate ko threat to protect the lower eye. The main chain's life was therefore also in serious jeopardy. Resignation was appropriate.

Do not describe this as established double-ko seki. Both vulnerable appendages were initially Black stones; after White takes one ko, Black cannot automatically capture at the other, already-owned ko as a response.

## What worked, within limits
- 37 B D1 forced 38 W B1 and secured a useful boundary point at the time.
- 39 B G4 required 41 B E4 after White F3 put F4/G4 in atari.
- 43 B F6 forced 44 W H5.
- 53 B D6 forced 54 W C7.
These local gains did not repair the opening's area deficit or the global eye problem.

## Next experiment
Keep the first move flexible; E5 was not disproved. Prioritize territory and eye space sooner, count both sides before the board becomes crowded, and reconsider contact exchanges that merely give the opponent a safe side group. A lower-ranked practice opponent is an option, but no training rank has been calibrated yet.

No external analysis engine or automated move recommendation was used. The review is manual and its proposed alternatives are unverified.

# Persistent Go learning

Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

## Record
- Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).
- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.
- Game 3: Black vs 8k, same rules. Lost by resignation after White move 64 (J5). Final captures: Black 1, White 2; no numerical final score.
- Game 4: White vs 12k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 43 (F1). Final captures: Black 1, White 0; no numerical final score.
- Read game-001.md for review. game-001.sgf is the full move record; game-001-log.json contains every returned position.
- Read game-002.md for the second review; game-002.sgf and game-002-log.json contain the complete record.
- Read game-003.md for the third review; game-003.sgf and game-003-log.json contain all 64 moves and returned positions.
- Read game-004.md for the latest review; game-004.sgf and game-004-log.json contain all 43 moves and returned positions.
- No successful level has been established. One loss does not establish individual move values.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.

## Next-game focus
- Choose a rank deliberately. Games against 9d, 4k, 8k and 12k were lost. Consider 20k next to establish basic living shapes and a successful baseline; it is an experiment, not an established best training rank. 9d remains the target.
- Keep opening alternatives as hypotheses. Securing a corner/lower-side position earlier (for example considering C3 before the upper-right exchanges) is worth trying, not established as best.
- Before each move: identify atari/cuts, weakest group and eye prospects, largest area gain, and whether opponent can ignore the intended threat.
- In contact fights, inspect current-board groups/liberties before EVERY move. Game 4 did this and addressed the J4/J5 atari, but still lost the main group. Use the inventory to assess eye space and escape routes as well as immediate atari.
- Name eye boundaries and the required dividing move before calling a group safe. Preserve both corner boundaries and outside liberties; an invading stone's capture may still leave only one eye.
- Count secure area and unsecured potential separately. Re-evaluate the base immediately after an undercut; do not defer it merely because the group has present liberties.
- Save complete move records, final result, and a small number of concrete lessons after each game. Update this file with the latest record and evidence.

## User constraints
Play each game to completion (passes or resignation allowed). Choose opponent before the first move.
Code may inspect the current board, count stones/liberties, check legality, and keep records. Do not build/use an engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or a program that selects/ranks/recommends moves.

# Game 2: White vs 4k — B+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, White komi 7, simple ko.
White resigned after move 49, Black J6. No numerical final score was produced.
4k was chosen as a territory-and-life training experiment after the game-1 loss against 9d. This loss does not establish a successful training rank.

## Full record
- game-002.sgf: all 49 stone moves, colors, opponent, rules, komi, result.
- game-002-log.json: every returned position and the resignation response.
- Final captures: Black 0, White 0. No ko occurred.

## Main failure: counting a base that did not exist
White began C3, C6, G3. The left-side framework was more territorial than game 1's central chain, but the lower-right group never secured two eyes. I counted prospective right-side area too generously and then treated extra connected stones as progress toward life.

Key sequence:
23 B G2, 24 W H2, 25 B F1, 26 W D2, 27 B H1, 28 W H3.
Black undercut the right group and occupied H1. White's H2/H3 connection did not secure the corner: H1 prevented J1 from functioning as an eye boundary. White should have re-evaluated the entire base at G2, and especially before playing elsewhere at move 26. Alternatives such as H3 instead of H2 need manual examination; this game does not establish their value.

37 B J4, 38 W J3, 39 B J5, 40 W G8.
The edge invasion occupied the remaining right-side eye space. The problem was already serious before J4; J4 was not merely a small territorial reduction. Starting another invasion did not rescue the first group.

42 W E4, 43 B F4.
I hoped E4 might separate the lower Black stones or help a connection. F4 connected F3 to F5 and removed a liberty of the right group. E4 did not force the intended separation.

At the final position, White G3/G4/G5/H2/H3/H5/J3 had exactly two liberties: H4 and J2.
Neither was an eye. Black H4 joins the large Black chain and leaves White J2 as its sole liberty. White J2 then exposes only J1; Black J1 captures the group. White cannot subsequently save it by J1: that fills its last liberty without capturing Black H1, which still has G1 available. Playing White H4 first likewise supplies no new liberty.
This is concrete local evidence for the group's failure, beyond a vague lack of eyes.

## Second invasion: too little room, too late
40 W G8, 41 B F8, 44 W H7, 45 B H9, 46 W G9, 48 W J8, 49 B J6.
White found a possible net against H9, but the three White components were still separate:
- G8/G9: liberties F9, G7, H8.
- H7: liberties G7, H8, J7.
- J8: liberties H8, J7, J9.

H8 would connect them and threaten H9. Capturing H9 would provide only one prospective eye; F9, G7, and J7 were boundary liberties that Black could contest. I had no demonstrated two-eye life or escape. A trapped enemy stone is not by itself a living invasion. The upper-right was not played out, so this review does not claim an engine-proven death.

## Missed immediate atari
47 B D3 left White D4/E4 with C4 as its ONLY liberty. I played 48 J8 without noticing this atari. C4 would connect D4/E4 to C3 and the main left group. It would not fix the overall loss, but ignoring a threatened two-stone group was a separate tactical mistake.

The final left group A5/B5/B6/C5/C6/D6/D7/E6/E7 had A4, B4, C4, C7 as liberties. Its access to the lower-left remained broad, but those liberties alone were not a proof of life. C3 and D2 were also separate stones, not a fully connected territorial boundary.

## What to carry forward
1. Run a current-board group/liberty inventory before moves in contact fights. This is allowed inspection, not move selection. In this game it would have exposed both the right group's shrinking liberties and D4/E4's atari.
2. Count unsecured side space separately from viable territory. A group lacking eyes or an escape must not contribute its whole surrounding region to an optimistic winning count.
3. Against an undercut, preserve the base before playing elsewhere. In particular, study the G2/H2/H1 sequence rather than assuming a connected second-line stone protects the corner.
4. Before invading, name the intended two eyes or a concrete connection route. The late upper-right invasion repeated the life problem in a smaller space.
5. Check the opponent's simplest connection: F4 joined F3 and F5. An adjacent attacking move does not force a cut.
6. A lower practice rank, for example 8k, is a reasonable next experiment to rehearse life and territory. It is not an established optimal rank; 9d remains the target.

All decisions and review were manual. Code only logged tool results, converted moves to SGF, and inspected the final board's groups and liberties. No engine, automated recommendations, or sequence-search program was used.

# Game 3: Black vs 8k — W+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Black resigned after move 64, White J5. The tool's next-move number was 65; only 64 stone moves were played. No numerical final score was produced.
8k was chosen to practise territory and life after losses against 9d and 4k. This game also lost; no successful practice rank is established.

## Records
- game-003.sgf: all 64 moves, colors, rules, komi, opponent and result.
- game-003-log.json: opponent selection, every play response and final resignation, with complete returned boards.
- Final captures: Black 1, White 2. No ko occurred.

## Main failure: enclosing groups without securing eyes
The opening C3/G3/E5 and subsequent contact play produced a lower framework. By move 16, the lower four rows alone were at most about 36 points, insufficient for Black's 45-point target when all points are assigned. The count prompted an upper-left entry, but I did not demonstrate its life. Later, another entry on the upper-right repeated the eye problem.

The initial lower framework was potential, not 36 secure points. White's later H3/H2/G2 and A3/A4/A2/A1/B1/C1 play reduced it substantially. At the final board the main lower Black group contained 17 stones. E1 was a true eye, and the enclosed D3/E3 region supplied another eye; this supported approximately 20 secure area, far short of a winning total. C2 and G1 should not simply be counted as secure extras.

## Upper-left: a base hypothesis that failed
17 B C8, 18 W B6, 19 B D8, 20 W E8,
21 B D7, 22 W E7, 23 B C7, 24 W A8,
25 B B7, 26 W A7, 27 B D9, 28 W E9.

After move 28, Black B7/C7/D7/C8/D8/D9 had only B8 and C9 as liberties. There was no demonstrated two-eye life or escape. D7/C7/B7 added connected stones along White's wall but did not secure a corner base. White A8/A7 and E9 took the boundaries needed for eyes.

At the final board, White A8 was connected to the main White group through A7/A6/B6. Thus the prospective top-left space B8/B9/C9 was not an enclosed three-point eye space: B8 bordered White A8. Merely splitting those empty points could not supply two true eyes. The group remained unrescued; it was not actually captured before resignation.

No single saving alternative is established by this record. Earlier top-edge or corner consolidation, or abandoning the entry sooner, needs manual consideration. Do not assume that C8 was proved wrong in isolation.

## Left-edge fight: two concrete reading errors
37 B B3, 38 W A4, 39 B A5, 40 W B5.
White B5 left Black A5 in atari with only A6. Black A6 was suicide: A5/A6 would have no liberties and would capture neither neighboring White group. I had considered the hane without adequately checking this cut.

41 B B4, 42 W A2, 43 B B2, 44 W A6 captured A5.
Removing A5 opened A5 as a NEW liberty for White A2/A3/A4. A planned squeeze down to A1 therefore no longer forced a capture. This repeats the earlier lesson that captures change adjacent liberties.

45 B A1, 46 W B1 captured A1.
The A1 throw-in was isolated, with B1 as its only liberty. White B1 both captured it and reopened A1 for the White edge stones. The throw-in did not seal the edge. Treat a move's own liberties and the opponent's simplest capture as mandatory checks, including on the first line.

## Upper-right: the decisive eye-shape mistake
29 B H7 and 33 B G7 entered while the region was relatively open. I then spent several turns elsewhere. White 54 G8 and 56 G9 narrowed the upper side.

55 B H8, 57 B H9, 58 W G6,
59 B H6, 60 W H5, 61 B J6, 62 W J8,
63 B J7, 64 W J5.

I incorrectly treated the empty strip J7/J8/J9 as adequate two-eye potential. A three-point strip is not already two eyes: ownership of its dividing point matters. After White J8, Black J7 was not a successful killing reply. White J5 removed the outside liberty of the entire Black group.

Final current-board inventory:
- Black G7/H6/H7/H8/H9/J6/J7: only J9 as a liberty.
- White J8: only J9 as a liberty.

If Black J9 captures J8, the resulting eight-stone Black group has only J8 as a liberty. White J8 then captures the whole group. This is legal and is not a ko: the recapture takes eight stones, not the single just-played stone. Capturing the invading stone would not restore life.

Do not simplify this to 'play J8 instead of J6 at move 61 and live.' At that time J6 was still open to an undercut, so the other boundary also needed protection. Earlier management of the corner and outside liberties was necessary; no complete saving variation was verified.

## What did work locally
31 B F3 connected G3 to the main group after White H3; the immediate two-liberty problem was addressed.
49 B D2 saved the ataried D1 stone after White C1 and connected it to E2.
51 B F2 joined the lower components, and 53 B F1 captured White E1, securing a real eye there. These local repairs did not offset the two failed upper groups.

## Next-game focus
1. Use a current-board group/liberty inventory before EVERY move in a contact fight, not just after a plan has failed. The inspection code was allowed and useful, but used too intermittently.
2. For each proposed eye, name its bordering stones and check that those stones connect and survive. For a three-point eye space, identify the dividing point and whether the opponent can take it first or undercut the boundary.
3. Rebuild liberties immediately after a capture, including sacrificed own stones. Do not reuse the old squeeze diagram.
4. Before a hane or throw-in, check the simplest cut/capture and the liberties of the new stone. The A5 and A1 moves are concrete reminders.
5. Count secure area separately from frameworks. Starting a second invasion does not make the first safe.
6. Consider 12k as the next tactical-and-life practice experiment. Losses against 9d, 4k and 8k have not established a successful rank. Keep 9d as the long-term target.

All moves and review were manual. Code logged responses, converted moves to SGF and inspected current-board groups/liberties. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move recommendation was used.

# Game 4: White vs 12k — B+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
White resigned after move 43, Black F1. The displayed next-move number was 44.
Final captures: Black 1, White 0. No ko or numerical final score.
12k was a practice experiment after losses against 9d, 4k and 8k; no successful rank is established.

## Records
- game-004.sgf: all 43 stone moves, colors, rules, opponent, komi and result.
- game-004-log.json: complete move list, opponent selection, every play response and resignation, including every returned board.
- A current-board group/liberty inventory was run after every play response. Code inspected only present groups and recorded moves; all decisions and this review were manual.

## Decisive result: thirteen stones with one eye space
After 42 W G1, 43 B F1, the White group comprised:
E6, F4, F5, F6, G1, G3, G4, H1, H2, H3, J3, J4, J5.
Its ONLY liberties were J1 and J2. Those adjacent points form one two-point eye space, not two eyes. The surrounding Black stones cut off every escape.

A concrete capture route is Black J2, leaving White J1 as its sole liberty. White J1 captures that single Black J2 stone, but the resulting fourteen-stone White group then has only J2. Black J2 captures all fourteen; this is not ko.
White J2 first instead leaves only J1; Black J1 captures the group directly.
A distant move would need to force an immediate rescue through capture; none was demonstrated. With the main group lost and only the much smaller left framework remaining, resignation was appropriate.

## The central extension did not remain an escape
The opening built a connected White C3-C8 wall, plus D8. It had substantial left-side potential, but not enough by itself to win. By move 15, the initial three-column framework represented only about 27 potential points, before reductions.

16 W H3, 17 B G2, 18 W H2, 19 B H4, 20 W H1.
H1 preserved the bottom boundary that had been lost in game 2, but did not supply a second eye. H4 blocked the upward right-side base. Preserving one boundary was useful locally and insufficient globally.

22 W G3, 24 W G4, 26 W F4, 28 W F5, 30 W F6, 32 W E6.
These extensions created a long connected group without enclosing eyes. The central route narrowed as Black played E5 and E4. E6 then added NO new empty neighboring point: D6, E5 and E7 were Black after 33 B E7, and F6 was White.

After the replies, the right group's liberties were:
- After 27 B E5: E4, F5, G1, G5, J1, J2, J3.
- After 29 B E4: F6, G1, G5, J1, J2, J3.
- After 31 B B2: E6, G1, G5, J1, J2, J3.
- After 33 B E7: G1, G5, J1, J2, J3.

The inventory was available, and I still proceeded through the narrowing route without a two-eye plan or a verified capture. At move 33 there was no direct route into open central space. G5 was bordered by White F5/G4 and Black G6/H5; occupying it would not open a new route. G1 offered only F1, which Black later blocked.
This game does not establish a single correct replacement move. Reconsider the H3/G2/H2/H4 exchanges and the F4-F5-F6-E6 plan earlier, rather than treating a later extension as an automatic rescue.

## Edge stones added size without restoring life
34 W J4, 36 W J5, 37 B J6 left J4/J5 in atari, with only J3. The inventory caught this, and 38 W J3 connected them to the main group.
39 B G5 then left the twelve-stone White group with only G1, J1 and J2. J3/J4/J5 were occupied stones; they had not become a second eye.

The right group grew from nine stones after move 33 to twelve after move 38, while the remaining eye space was still J1/J2. Adding connected edge stones did not repair the base.

## The last threat could be answered by capturing its new stone
Before 40 W G7, Black G5/G6/H4/H5 had G7 and H6 as its two liberties.
White G7 threatened that group but was itself in atari, with ONLY G8. Black 41 G8 captured it immediately.

Removing White G7 reopened G7 for three neighboring Black groups: G5/G6/H4/H5, D6/D7/E7/E8/F7, and H7. The threat therefore did not force Black H6 or win a capture.
This was a desperate attempt with a visible refutation, not evidence for a useful forcing move. A threat that the opponent can answer by capturing the threatening stone must be evaluated on the resulting board.

42 W G1 briefly exposed F1 as an external liberty. 43 B F1 removed it and produced the final one-eye position.

## Other strategic issue
21 B C2 and 31 B B2 undercut the original left framework while White worked on the right. The original approximately 27-point count was no longer valid. The final seven-stone left group still had broad left/top space, but its whole surrounding region was not established secure territory, and it could not compensate for the thirteen-stone loss.

## Carry forward
1. Keep the inventory before every contact move; it prevented an ignored atari here. Add a deliberate eye-and-escape assessment: where does the next extension actually reach open space?
2. Re-evaluate immediately when the last central route narrows to one point. F6 had only E6 as a new direction; E6 was surrounded after E7. Many total liberties hid the absence of a viable escape.
3. Name BOTH eyes and their surviving boundary chains before spending several moves enlarging a corner group. H1 saved a boundary but H4 had already restricted the upper base.
4. Do not count occupied edge stones as eye space. J3/J4/J5 enlarged the group while J1/J2 remained its single eye region.
5. Check whether a capture threat can be answered by capturing its new stone, and then rebuild all adjacent liberties.
6. Consider 20k next to establish basic living shapes and a successful baseline. Four losses do not identify an optimal training rank or prove specific opening moves wrong. 9d remains the target.

No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or automated move ranking/recommendation was used.
